stem.en: A piston at one end of a long tube of air is pushed forward, pulled back, then pushed forward again. What happens in the tube?

text.en: Each push makes a region of higher density and each pull a region of lower density, and both travel along the tube.
Each push makes a region of lower density and each pull a region of higher density, and both travel along the tube.
Each push carries the air next to the piston all the way to the far end of the tube.
Each push moves all the air in the tube along at once, as one solid block.

explanation.en: Pushing the piston forward packs the air next to it closer than average: a compression, a region of higher density. Pulling it back lets that air spread out more than average: a rarefaction, a region of lower density. The particles push on the particles ahead of them, so each region travels along the tube, while the particles themselves only vibrate about their own places.

hints.en: When the piston moves forward, the same particles have less room. Are they packed closer or more spread out?
Does the air next to the piston ever reach the far end, or does only the change in density travel?
